What is happening and how do I fix it?", "type": "text"}], "created_at": null}
{"id": "23849be4-c6f6-4c32-a79b-1c7332dd572d", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"type": "chat_title", "title": "Ubuntu apt upgrade kept back packages not installing"}]}

{"id": "434a0f18-3a8c-46f3-a6c5-4bf8255bd28b", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"text": "This is a classic apt-upgrade behavior, not an error — let me walk through what's happening and how to fix it.

**What's going on**

`apt upgrade` (the non-dash-dash-full version) deliberately refuses to install upgrades that would require adding or removing packages — it only applies upgrades that can be satisfied with the exact set of packages already installed. If a security update bumps a dependency (new library version, a new recommended package, a changed Depends/Breaks relationship, or a kernel/meta-package pulling in a new ABI package), apt won't silently add those packages. Instead it just reports the package as "kept back" and skips it, with no error.

This commonly happens with:
- Kernel updates (new `linux-image-*` ABI package needs to be installed alongside/replacing the old one)
- Packages where a new version adds a dependency not currently installed
- Packages held via `apt-mark hold` (less likely here since you said "several" security updates all behaving this way, but worth ruling out)

**How to fix it**

1. Check if anything is explicitly held:
   ```
   apt-mark showhold
   ```
   If packages show up here, unhold with `sudo apt-mark unhold <package>`.

2. If nothing is held, the fix is to let apt resolve the new dependencies by using full-upgrade (equivalent to `dist-upgrade`):
   ```
   sudo apt update
   sudo apt full-upgrade
   ```
   This allows apt to install/remove packages as needed to satisfy the upgrade, which is exactly what's needed when a new dependency appears.

3. Alternatively, if you only want to force specific packages without a full upgrade:
   ```
   sudo apt install <package1> <package2> ...
   ```
   Explicitly naming the kept-back packages in an `install` command lets apt pull in whatever new dependencies are required for just those.

4. Always review before applying — run with `-s` (simulate) first if you want to confirm what will change:
   ```
   apt full-upgrade -s
   ```

For unattended security patching specifically, `unattended-upgrades` by default only applies updates that don't require new dependencies either, so you may see the same "kept back" packages recur there too — in that case periodically running `full-upgrade` manually (or scheduling it) is the way to catch them.

Want me to check whether any packages in your environment are currently on hold, or look at a specific instance's apt state?", "type": "text"}], "created_at": null}
